## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Indriyajātaka* (Ja 423) is a canonical birth story in the Pali *Jātaka* collection. The narrative opening preserved in the commentary records that the Buddha spoke this tale while residing at Jetavana concerning a monk's temptation by the wife of his former days (*purāṇadutiyikāpalobhana*), beginning with the line *Yo indriyānaṁ* (“Who through desire”) [Fausböll 1883]. In the past story, the Bodhisatta is an ascetic teacher with seven chief disciples; six of them—including the eldest, the future Sāriputta—depart to establish independent hermitages, while Anusissa (the future Ānanda) stays behind to serve as his attendant, anticipating their subsequent relationship in their final lives [Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Doctrinally, the verses treat themes of equanimity, self-restraint, and steadfastness in the face of gain and misfortune (*ahāso atthalābhesu, atthavyāpatti avyatho*), framed by an episode where an ascetic falls in love with a courtesan and is admonished by his brother [Anandajoti 2010].
